records.name_note: NC State Extension and UGA Extension both use the one-word form 'Switchgrass', while Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder gives the two-word form 'switch grass' as its primary common name -- a spelling/spacing variation across sources for the same species.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail were left null: the only pet/animal-safety information found in admissible sources is UGA Extension's caution (Bulletin B-1358) that switchgrass hay may cause excessive hair loss and sun sensitivity in horses — this names horses only, not cats or dogs, so per the schema rules it cannot support toxic_to_pets=true. No admissible source discusses cat or dog toxicity for this species at all: NC State's Plant Toolbox page has no Poison/toxicity tags, and Missouri Botanical Garden's profile mentions none either.

water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis were left null: admissible sources describe this species' moisture tolerance only in general landscape terms (e.g., Missouri Botanical Garden's 'Water: Medium to wet'; NC State's Soil Drainage tags spanning Moist, Occasionally Wet, Occasionally Dry, and Occasional Flooding), not as a container-style watering cadence, dry-down depth, or day-interval schedule, so none of these fields could be populated.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength were left null: the only fertilization guidance found in admissible sources (UGA Extension Bulletin B-1358) gives per-acre nitrogen rates for agricultural biomass/forage/hay production (e.g., 50-75 lb N/acre applied within two weeks of spring green-up), which the schema explicitly excludes from fertilize_strength as a per-area application rate rather than a liquid-feed dilution fraction. The bulletin also never names a literal day-count interval or specific calendar months, so those fields could not be populated either.

light_fc_min, light_fc_good, and direct_sun_hours_max were left null: NC State Extension gives hour-based thresholds for classifying Full sun (6+ hours) versus Partial Shade (2-6 hours) light categories, but no admissible source reports foot-candle light readings, and none frame an upper hour limit beyond which the plant is harmed, so direct_sun_hours_max is not well supported in that framing.

day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, chill_damage_f, and cool_rest_note were left null: this species is an outdoor, winter-hardy perennial grass (USDA zones 5a-9b per NC State; RHS hardiness H5) grown in the ground, not a houseplant kept in controlled indoor temperature/humidity. No admissible source frames its cold tolerance as a specific chill-damage threshold temperature or discusses ambient humidity needs.

outdoor_sun_exposure includes part_shade despite one dissenting note: University of Maryland Extension states switchgrass 'does not tolerate much shade and grows best in full sun,' but this is outweighed by NC State's, Missouri Botanical Garden's, and UGA Extension's explicit statements that the species tolerates partial shade (with some loss of upright form), so part_shade was retained per the weight of admissible-source evidence.

soil_base was set to garden_bed based on this species being described throughout admissible sources as an in-ground landscape/meadow/prairie plant (borders, wild gardens, meadows, woodlands). NC State also lists 'Container' among possible landscape locations, but given the plant's outdoor hardiness rating and the lack of any potting-mix-specific guidance in any admissible source, garden_bed remains the better-supported enum value rather than standard_potting.

RHS's structured tags describe Soil pH only qualitatively as 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' with no numeric range, so RHS could not be used for soil_ph_min/max; the numeric range (5.0-8.0) instead comes from UGA Extension's Bulletin B-1358.

The sub-claim is nonetheless true and simply uncited-but-true under this field: UGA Bulletin B-1358's title reads 'The Management and Use of Switchgrass in Georgia' and its body opens 'Switchgrass is a native warm season (NWS) perennial grass that can be grown throughout Georgia and most of the United States' (verified verbatim in the live PDF). day_f_min / day_f_max / night_f_min / night_f_max: no admissible source gives an ambient day/night temperature range; only USDA hardiness-zone winter-survival data exists, and it disagrees across sources (Clemson zones 7-10; NC State zones 5a-9b; UF/IFAS zones 7-11; Missouri Botanical Garden zones 5-11). Per established convention, zone survival data is not mapped onto ambient day/night temperature fields.

chill_damage_f: no admissible source states a specific damage-onset cold temperature. RHS gives a Hardiness Rating of H4 (-10 to -5°C), but that is a winter-survival rating, not the damage-onset figure this field calls for.
cool_rest_note: no admissible source discusses a dormancy or chilling requirement for this species.

humidity_need / humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max: Clemson states the plant 'Tolerates heat, humidity, drought, and poor soil,' which describes tolerance of humidity, not a specific need or level, so it does not resolve to the low/average/high enum. No source gives a percentage.
light_fc_min / light_fc_good: no admissible source gives foot-candle light values for this species.

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' defines the minimum threshold for its Full Sun category, not a maximum sun-hour ceiling, so it cannot be used for this field.

soil_drainage: NC State's own structured Soil Drainage tags for this species are 'Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry, Very Dry' -- it carries 'Occasionally Dry' alongside 'Good Drainage' (partially matching the 'moderate' pattern) but lacks the literal 'Occasionally Wet' tag that category requires, and the presence of 'Occasionally Dry' rules out 'moisture_retentive' (which requires no occasionally-dry counterpart). Missouri Botanical Garden separately lists 'Water: Dry to medium' and UF/IFAS lists 'extended flooding' tolerance alongside 'high' drought tolerance -- real wet-and-dry tolerance that rules out 'fast' (which requires no wet-tolerance) -- but none of this cleanly resolves to one of the three enum tokens as strictly defined, so left null rather than guessed.

soil_ph_min / soil_ph_max: NC State's Soil pH tags span 'Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0), Alkaline (>8.0)' -- essentially the plant's full practical tolerance range with no distinguishing numeric bound narrower than that; no admissible source gives a tighter target range.

water_regime / water_dry_down_target / water_check_depth_cm / water_growing_days_est / water_dormant_days_est / water_estimate_basis: this is an outdoor garden-bed/rain-garden ornamental grass, not framed as a container plant by any admissible source. Sources describe garden-bed watering only in general terms (Missouri Botanical Garden 'Water: Dry to medium'; Clemson 'somewhat drought tolerant once established... will look better and flower more profusely with periodic supplemental irrigation during periods of drought') that do not map onto the container-oriented water_regime categories or give a numeric interval, check-depth, or dormancy-duration estimate.

fertilize_interval_days / fertilize_active_months / fertilize_strength: no admissible source specifies a fertilizing schedule or dilution rate. UF/IFAS instead frames the species as needing minimal care ('There are no known pests or problems') and Missouri Botanical Garden lists 'Maintenance: Low.'

outdoor_sun_exposure: full_shade was excluded because no admissible source describes shade tolerance beyond 'light shade'/'part shade'/'partial shade'; only full_sun and part_shade are well-supported.

Common-name overlap: Clemson, NC State, and UF/IFAS all list overlapping alternate names (Gulf Muhly, Gulf Muhly Grass, Sweetgrass, Purple Muhly) for M. capillaris that are also the primary common names of the distinct species Muhlenbergia sericea (see name_note) -- a real risk that a buyer sourcing by common name alone could get the other species.

USDA hardiness zone figures vary by source (Clemson 7-10; NC State 5a-9b; UF/IFAS 7-11; Missouri Botanical Garden 5-11); no schema field captures hardiness zone directly so this was not resolved, only noted for completeness.

records.name_note: NC State Extension's own page for Phlox subulata itself also tags it 'Creeping Phlox' alongside 'Moss Phlox' -- the name is used ambiguously for both this species and the different, shade-loving woodland species Phlox stolonifera within NC State's own taxonomy, not cleanly reserved for one or the other. Clemson HGIC, however, does cleanly separate the two: its factsheet covers Phlox subulata as 'Moss Phlox' and Phlox stolonifera as 'Creeping Phlox' in distinct sections with no name overlap. Missouri Botanical Garden designates 'moss phlox' as this species' primary common name, and RHS likewise designates 'moss phlox', listing flowering moss, ground pink, moss pink, mountain pink, and rock phlox as further alternates -- without creeping phlox among them. Previously known as Phlox brittonii and Phlox setacea.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox tags Phlox subulata as non-toxic to cats, dogs, and horses; no admissible source describes any toxic principle, plant part, or ingestion symptoms for this species.
unknowns: chill_damage_f / cool_rest_note: no admissible source states a specific cold-damage-onset temperature or a chilling/dormancy requirement for Phlox subulata. Sources give only USDA Hardiness Zone survival ranges (NC State 3a-9b; Missouri Botanical Garden Zone 3-9; RHS Hardiness H6, -20 to -15C; Penn State Extension Zones 3-9), which describe winter survival rather than a damage-onset temperature, so both fields were left null.

day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: not addressed by any admissible source -- this is an outdoor garden groundcover, and none of the consulted sources frame its care in terms of daytime/nighttime degree-Fahrenheit targets.

humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: not addressed by any admissible source. NC State notes 'nematodes can cause damage to the leaves in wet and humid conditions,' but this describes a disease-risk condition, not a humidity care target, so it was not used to fill these fields.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good: no footcandle figures given by any admissible source; sun requirements are described only via categorical terms (full sun / dappled sun / partial shade), consistent with this being an outdoor plant rather than an indoor houseplant.

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's tag states a MINIMUM sun requirement ('Full sun: 6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day'), not a maximum; no admissible source gives a sun-hours ceiling for this sun-loving species, so this field (framed as a ceiling) was left null.

water_regime: left null despite Clemson ('withstands drought once established...will not tolerate excessive moisture') and UGA CAES ('very heat and drought tolerant but very intolerant of poor drainage') both suggesting a dry-leaning regime, because Missouri Botanical Garden's own structured tag for this species reads 'Water: Medium' (not Dry or Dry-to-medium), and no admissible source gives an explicit watering-between-waterings instruction for this species -- only general drought-establishment language. Given the tension between the structured tag and the prose, and no explicit cadence stated anywhere, this was left null rather than resolved to a specific token.

water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_check_depth_cm/water_dry_down_target/water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives any numeric watering-interval, check-depth, or dry-down-target figures for this species.

fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_active_months/fertilize_strength: none of the admissible sources consulted (NC State, Missouri Botanical Garden, Clemson HGIC, RHS, Penn State Extension, University of Maryland Extension, UGA CAES Field Report) give a fertilizing schedule, dilution rate, or interval for Phlox subulata specifically.

soil_ph: University of Maryland Extension's structured tag gives the numeric range used here ('pH 5.7-7.5'). NC State's own structured field separately lists 'Soil pH: Acid (<6.0)' as one tolerance category while also carrying a free-text tag '#neutral pH' elsewhere on the same page -- the two NC State signals aren't fully reconciled with each other, but both fall inside the wider UMD-sourced 5.7-7.5 range, so UMD's explicit numeric range was used and NC State's categorical tags were treated as broadly consistent background rather than a conflicting numeric source.

soil_drainage: classified as fast on the strength of Clemson's explicit 'will not tolerate excessive moisture' and UGA CAES's explicit 'very intolerant of poor drainage,' but NC State's own structured Soil Drainage tags for this species list 'Good Drainage,' 'Moist,' AND 'Occasionally Dry' together -- the 'Moist' tag sits in some tension with a fast-drainage classification. Two independent sources state outright intolerance of wet/poor-drainage conditions against one ambiguously-tagged source, so fast was retained as the better-supported reading rather than left null.

common_name/name_note: 'Creeping Phlox,' the name used to frame this research task, is genuinely ambiguous among the admissible sources -- both NC State Extension and Clemson HGIC use 'Creeping Phlox' as the common name for a DIFFERENT species, Phlox stolonifera (a shade-loving woodland groundcover), not Phlox subulata. 'Moss Phlox' was chosen as common_name because it is the source-designated primary name at Missouri Botanical Garden and RHS.

outdoor_sun_exposure: full_sun and part_shade are both well supported (NC State's 'Dappled Sunlight' tag maps to part_shade per catalog convention; RHS lists 'Partial shade'; Penn State Extension notes it 'also grows in light shade'). Clemson notes shade causes plants to thin out and that the species 'cannot tolerate excessive shade,' but this describes intolerance of heavy/full shade specifically, not a rejection of the part_shade category, so full_shade was excluded while part_shade was retained.

Genus-bleed check: confirmed no content from Phlox paniculata (Garden Phlox, the taller upright species already covered in this catalog's b17-perennials3.json) was used in this record. All data traces to sources' Phlox-subulata-specific sections -- verified Clemson's 'Moss Phlox (Phlox subulata)' subsection specifically, which is distinct on the same multi-species factsheet page from its 'Garden Phlox,' 'Hairy Phlox,' and 'Creeping Phlox [Phlox stolonifera]' subsections.

name_note — removed on audit: Fetched the live NC State Extension page for Phlox subulata itself (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/phlox-subulata/, the exact URL cited elsewhere in this record for is_houseplant/toxicity/'previously known as'). Its own <title> and on-page H1/H2 read: 'Phlox subulata (Creeping Phlox, Flowering Moss, Ground Pink, Moss Phlox, Moss Pink, Moss-pink, Mountain Pink, Rock Phlox)' and, under the 'Common Name(s):' heading, the FIRST listed tag is a link to '/plants/phlox-subulata/common-name/creeping-phlox/' labeled 'Creeping Phlox.' So NC State Extension does NOT reserve 'Creeping Phlox' exclusively for Phlox stolonifera -- it also tags Phlox subulata itself with that name, on the very page this record cites repeatedly for other fields. This directly falsifies the record's name_note sentence 'NC State Extension and Clemson HGIC both also use the common name "Creeping Phlox" for a different, shade-loving woodland species, Phlox stolonifera -- not for Phlox subulata specifically' -- that clause is true for Clemson but false for NC State. Breaking down the bundled sub-claims: (1) 'NC State Extension uses Creeping Phlox as the common name for... Phlox stolonifera' -- the underlying quote ('Phlox stolonifera (Creeping Phlox, Star Rock Phlox)') is verbatim-accurate for the stolonifera page, but the surrounding 'not for Phlox subulata specifically' framing is WRONG and should be dropped/corrected, not re-cited as-is -- it needs to say NC State applies 'Creeping Phlox' to BOTH species, i.e. it's an ambiguous tag within NC State's own taxonomy, not a clean disambiguator. (2) 'Clemson HGIC also uses Creeping Phlox... for Phlox stolonifera, in the same factsheet that separately covers Phlox subulata as Moss Phlox' -- CONFIRMED ACCURATE: Clemson's factsheet at hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/phlox/ has a distinct 'Moss Phlox (Phlox subulata)' section under 'Low Sun Loving Phlox' and a separate 'Creeping Phlox (Phlox stolonifera)' section under 'Low Shade Loving Phlox,' with no bleed of the 'creeping phlox' name into the subulata section. (3) 'Missouri Botanical Garden designates moss phlox as the primary common name' -- CONFIRMED ACCURATE: MOBOT's page has a singular 'Common Name: moss phlox' field (raw HTML verified) distinct from its 'Common Names' alternates tooltip (flowering moss, ground pink, moss pink, mountain pink, rock phlox), and 'creeping phlox' appears nowhere on that page. (4) 'RHS designates moss phlox... listing flowering moss, ground pink, moss pink, mountain pink, rock phlox as Other common names -- without creeping phlox among them' -- CONFIRMED ACCURATE via raw HTML (RHS page <title> is 'Phlox subulata | moss phlox'; 'Other common names' list matches exactly, no creeping phlox). (5) 'previously known as Phlox brittonii and Phlox setacea' -- CONFIRMED ACCURATE, verbatim match to NC State's 'Previously known as:' section. Net effect: sub-claims 2-5 are fine and should be kept; sub-claim 1 (the NC-State-exclusivity clause) is factually wrong and should be corrected to reflect that NC State's own naming is internally ambiguous/overlapping between the two species rather than cleanly separated, which weakens (though does not overturn, since Clemson/MOBOT/RHS still independently support 'Moss Phlox') the record's stated rationale for preferring 'Moss Phlox' as common_name.

records.name_note: RHS's dedicated species page for Portulaca grandiflora lists "moss rose" only within a secondary "Other common names" field alongside six other synonyms (eleven o'clock, Kentucky moss, large-flowered purslane, Mexican rose, sun plant, wax pink) -- it is not the page's own lead common name, which is "rose moss". This record therefore uses "rose moss", not "moss rose", as common_name, even though "moss rose" remains a very widely used name for the same plant (including in the research brief that prompted this record).
unknowns: toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail: no admissible source (NC State, Clemson HGIC, Missouri Botanical Garden, RHS, UF/IFAS ask.ifas.ufl.edu, Penn State Extension, UMD Extension, UGA CAES Field Report) discusses Portulaca grandiflora's toxicity to cats or dogs in either direction. A non-admissible ASPCA page found in general web search lists this species as non-toxic to cats/dogs, but ASPCA is not on the admissible-domain list, so it was not used and toxic_to_pets is left null rather than inferred from it.

chill_damage_f / cool_rest_note: RHS gives only a hardiness-rating survival floor for the species (H2: 'tolerant of low temperatures, but not surviving being frozen', 1 to 5 degrees C) -- a class-level tolerance/survival threshold, not a stated frost/cold damage-onset temperature -- and no admissible source discusses a dormancy or cool-rest period for this annual, so both fields are left null.
day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: no admissible source gives a specific daytime or nighttime growing-temperature range in degrees for this species.
humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: not addressed by any admissible source for this outdoor bedding annual.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good/direct_sun_hours_max: sources describe light only as a sun-exposure category ('Full sun'), and NC State's own definition of that category is an open-ended '6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day' -- a generic, site-wide category threshold reused across plant profiles, not a species-specific maximum or a footcandle figure -- so none of these numeric fields were populated.

soil_base: this species is grown both in garden beds/rock gardens (Missouri Botanical Garden: 'rock gardens or along walks'; RHS: 'Rock garden', 'Gravel garden') and in containers/hanging baskets (Missouri Botanical Garden: 'Containers, hanging baskets'; NC State tags '#container plant' and '#hanging baskets'; RHS: 'Patio and container plants'), so no single soil_base token applies cleanly without guessing; left null.

soil_ph_min: NC State's structured Soil pH field checks 'Acid (<6.0)' for this species, but that category is open-ended with no stated lower-bound number, so only the 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' category's upper bound (8.0) could be taken numerically, giving soil_ph_max alone.

soil_drainage tension: NC State Extension's own structured 'Soil Drainage' tag for this species is 'Good Drainage' plus 'Occasionally Wet' with no 'Occasionally Dry' tag, which under this schema's enum rule maps to moisture_retentive. This sits in tension with the same NC State page's own '#drought tolerant' tag and with Missouri Botanical Garden's independent 'Water: Dry to medium' / 'Tolerate: Drought, Dry Soil' characterization, and with Clemson HGIC listing Moss Rose repeatedly under 'Annuals for Hot, Dry Locations' and 'Annuals for Poor Soil' rather than its separate 'Annuals for Moist Soil' list. Recorded as moisture_retentive per the literal structured-tag rule, but flagged here given the conflicting drought-tolerant framing elsewhere.

water_regime: Missouri Botanical Garden gives 'Water: Dry to medium' and its Culture notes describe 'poor to average, dry to moderately moist, well-drained soils... Drought tolerant,' but this qualitative language does not resolve unambiguously to one of the four enum tokens, so water_regime was left null rather than guessed.

water_dry_down_target/water_check_depth_cm/water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives a watering interval, a soil-check depth, or day-count/dormancy data for this species.

fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_active_months/fertilize_strength: Clemson HGIC's Growing Annuals page gives a general fertilization schedule (a complete slow-release 12-6-6 fertilizer, reapplied 'at 6 week intervals') but this is generic guidance for annual bedding plants as a category on a page listing dozens of species, not information specific to Portulaca grandiflora; no admissible source gives a species-specific fertilizing schedule or dilution strength, so these fields are left null.

common_name resolution: NC State Extension's own dedicated page lists five common names together (Moss Rose, Portulaca, Purslane, Rose Moss, Sun Plant) with no indicated lead name, so the common_name tie-break relied on Missouri Botanical Garden and RHS, whose dedicated single-species pages both explicitly lead with 'rose moss' while relegating 'moss rose' to a secondary/plural names field.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: The citation's quote ('Soil Drainage: Good Drainage Occasionally Wet') is accurately reproduced from NC State's live page, and the record's literal-tag mapping technically follows the moderate-vs-moisture_retentive disambiguation rule. But the chosen VALUE 'moisture_retentive' is contradicted by the weight of evidence, including a stronger, more specific data point the record did not weigh: NC State's own page states elsewhere, in plain prose, 'Poorly drained soils may lead to crown rot' -- a direct, same-source warning that wet/poorly-drained soil actively harms this plant, which is inconsistent with a moisture-retentive-soil recommendation. This sits alongside NC State's own '#drought tolerant', '#succulent', and '#cactus' hashtag tags and its description that it 'needs to be planted in well-drained sandy or rocky soils'; Missouri Botanical Garden's independent 'Water: Dry to medium', 'Tolerate: Drought, Dry Soil', and 'Good for poor dry soils where many other plants struggle'; Clemson HGIC listing it under 'Annuals for Hot, Dry Locations' and 'Annuals for Poor Soil' rather than 'Annuals for Moist Soil'; and RHS's soil types ('Chalk, Loam, Sand') with no moisture-retentive soil type listed. Five independent lines of evidence, including a same-source disease-risk statement, converge on this being a fast-draining-soil plant. Recommending 'moisture_retentive' soil in a care app risks real harm (crown rot) rather than being a defensible edge-case call -- the better-supported value is 'fast' (or, if the tension is judged irreconcilable, null rather than an affirmatively wrong enum value). The record's own unknowns entry candidly flags this tension but still lands on the value the evidence weighs against.

normalizations: 2026-08-23: twenty-third batch -- five ornamental grasses (Maiden Grass, Switchgrass, Pink Muhly Grass, Japanese Sedge, Blue Fescue, a genuinely thin category until now), Hardy Ice Plant, Moss Phlox (deliberately researched as a companion to the taller border Phlox species already covered; no genus-content bleed found), and Rose Moss. This batch's common_name and array-field manual-review flags (added after b39/b40) caught one more real defect: Hardy Ice Plant's record picked 'Hardy Ice Plant' from NC State's page title, but that page's own title actually lists 'Cooper's Hardy Ice Plant' first and 'Hardy Ice Plant' second -- the record used the secondary name, not the lead one -- corrected to "Cooper's Hardy Ice Plant" using the same citation. Five more name_note repairs, all adding a citation for a sub-claim the auditor independently confirmed true but uncited, following this catalog's established per-sub-claim repair discipline: Switchgrass gained a UGA Extension citation for its one-word-spelling sub-claim; Pink Muhly Grass gained a Clemson citation for its shared-common-names-with-M.-sericea sub-claim; Hardy Ice Plant gained a UF/IFAS citation establishing both this species and the name-colliding Carpobrotus edulis share family Aizoaceae. Moss Phlox's name_note needed an actual correction, not just a citation add: the audit found NC State's own dedicated Phlox subulata page tags this exact species with 'Creeping Phlox' too (not just the different species Phlox stolonifera as the record had claimed), directly contradicting the record's 'not for Phlox subulata specifically' framing -- reworded to describe NC State's own naming as internally ambiguous/overlapping between the two species (true), while keeping the record's still-accurate observations that Clemson, MOBOT, and RHS each cleanly designate 'Moss Phlox' as the primary name with no such overlap. Rose Moss's soil_drainage was corrected from 'moisture_retentive' to 'fast' after the audit found the record's literal NC-State-tag mapping ('Good Drainage, Occasionally Wet' -> moisture_retentive per this catalog's refined convention) was outweighed by five independent lines of evidence -- including a same-source explicit crown-rot warning ('Poorly drained soils may lead to crown rot') plus consistent dry/drought framing across NC State, MOBOT, Clemson, and RHS -- a case where the mechanical tag-mapping rule and the weight of qualitative evidence pointed opposite directions and the evidence should win, especially given the real crown-rot harm risk a wrong 'moisture_retentive' recommendation could cause. Rose Moss's common_name was also normalized from lowercase 'rose moss' (the literal source-page casing) to Title Case 'Rose Moss' for consistency with this catalog's existing capitalization convention -- a cosmetic fix, not a correction of substance. None of the eight species in this batch had any admissible cat/dog-scoped toxicity evidence except Moss Phlox, cleanly false via explicit NC State '#non-toxic for cats'/'#non-toxic for dogs' tags.
